cultivar: Zao Bai Jian (early-budding local selection) and Sichuan medium-leaf population bushes
processing: Fully oxidised gongfu black: a bud with one or two leaves is withered, rolled, oxidised and dried, then sorted; the early spring 'Zao Bai Jian' lots are made from the very first buds.
harvest_season: The earliest black-tea harvest in China: first buds in late February or early March in Yibin's warm valleys, with the main spring picking through March and April.
appearance_dry: Tight, slim, slightly curved dark strands with golden tips, the early lots almost all bud.
appearance_wet: Even copper-red leaves and buds, tender and glossy.
taste_profile: Smooth and sweet with a distinctive orange-candy note over malt and cocoa, soft tannin and a clean finish.

brewing.notes: Gaiwan at around 90 °C, short steeps; the early bud lots prefer slightly cooler water. Western-style: 3 g per 250 ml, 3 minutes.

vintage_note: Sold as the current year's spring harvest, and the early-March 'Zao Bai Jian' lots are the ones that command a premium because they reach the market weeks before any other Chinese black; drink within a year. Not aged.
description:
Chuan Hong is Sichuan's gongfu black, made around Yibin in the south of the province where the Min and Jinsha rivers meet to form the Yangtze. It is a product of the 1950s, when Sichuan's tea industry was pointed at the export market and Yibin's warm, low river valleys turned out to have a trick nobody else could match: tea buds appear there in late February, so Chuan Hong is the first black tea of every Chinese year.

The tea is made in the standard gongfu way – withered, rolled, oxidised, dried and sorted – from a bud with one or two leaves. The flagship early lots use Zao Bai Jian, 'early white tip', a local selection chosen for budding first, and they are nearly all bud. The local leaf has a characteristic sweetness that Chinese tasters describe as orange candy, which is as good a description as any.

In the cup expect that orange-sweet note over malt and cocoa, a soft tannin and a clean, slightly brisk finish; it runs six or seven steeps at around 90 °C and makes a friendly, undemanding pot. It is a gentler tea than Yunnan black and a rounder one than Keemun, and it is at its best drunk neat and fresh.

It is sold as the current spring, and the first-of-the-year lots are priced for their novelty as much as their quality; the main March–April picking is better value and often better tea. Look for slim, tight, tippy leaf and a sweet citrus-and-malt dry aroma; the rest of Sichuan also makes black tea now, often from the same cultivars, so 'Chuan Hong' on a label does not always mean Yibin.

If you miss the first spring greens, a packet of early Chuan Hong is the next best way to drink the new year's tea in March.
sources_note: The 'orange candy aroma' (橘糖香) descriptor and the late-February first picking are from Chinese trade descriptions; the 1950s start of commercial production (export to the USSR) is the standard account.
